e-5528.knowledge_point: Finding a Complex Eigenvalue of a Matrix Given a Complex Eigenvector
e-5528.problem:
Determine whether ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14041802/assets/59af73d1cda1a988c775ccf198b53653b96660b4ad8416add1b0c1816e89a5a5.png) is an eigenvector of the matrix ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14041802/assets/963bcaf94bc481fe8fbc99ca28fba037047d8821661eadcf0e5e9ce50ba39ef8.png)
If so, then what is the corresponding eigenvalue?
e-5528.worked_solution:
The eigenvectors of $A$ are the non-zero vectors $\mathbf{v}$ such that $A\mathbf{v}=\lambda \mathbf{v}.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Av & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -5 \\ 8 & -2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1+3\text{i} \\ 4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-18+6\text{i} \\ 24\text{i}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}18{\text{i}}^{2}+6\text{i} \\ 24\text{i}\end{aligned}] \\  & =6\text{i}[\begin{aligned}1+3\text{i} \\ 4\end{aligned}] \\  & =6\text{i}v.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $A\mathbf{v} = 6\textrm{i} \mathbf{v},$ we conclude that $\mathbf{v}$ is an eigenvector of $A$ and the corresponding eigenvalue is $\lambda=6\textrm{i}.$

e-5527.knowledge_point: Finding a Complex Eigenvector of a Matrix Given a Complex Eigenvalue
e-5527.problem:
Find an eigenvector of 
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14041802/assets/7dad070080562e459c926f5c8fa3d71a56981d68bd3ed4aae768c2f7450685a3.png)
that corresponds to the eigenvalue $\lambda=-3+4\textrm{i}.$
e-5527.worked_solution:
To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation 

$$
(A - \lambda I) \textbf{x}=\mathbf{0}.
$$

 

In our case, we have $\,\lambda =-3+4\textrm{i},$ and

$$
\begin{aligned}A-\lambda I & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & 4 \\ -4 & -3\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}-3+4\text{i} & 0 \\ 0 & -3+4\text{i}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-4\text{i} & 4 \\ -4 & -4\text{i}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the homogeneous system of linear equations

$$
{\begin{aligned}-4\text{i}{x}_{1}+4{x}_{2}=0 \\ -4{x}_{1}-4\text{i}{x}_{2}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since the matrix $A-(-3+4\textrm{i})I$ is singular, the system above must have a non-zero solution. This means that one equation of the system is a multiple of another.

As a result, we can drop one of the rows and take one of the variables to be the free variable. For example, from the second equation, we get

$$
x_1 = -\textrm{i}x_2.
$$

Therefore, the general solution is given by

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14041802/assets/6786c7bc4d12bc3ee1a335eeb45967475850a585ec36805fe81aa76360d5a729.png)

Setting $x_2=1,$ we get the eigenvector ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14041802/assets/a73682dbe1dfccc14e5b3f0c68aa6e6aa7eb7a67bb475efbbaeaa1e886585554.png)

e-5529.knowledge_point: Finding Two Linearly Independent Complex Eigenvectors of a 2x2 Matrix
e-5529.problem:
Let ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14041802/assets/e6a0d43572790d4daa49659c271c17032f2601458db0f6843257df07c245f372.png) and ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14041802/assets/9bf515d20e5a19646680474f0243dba793d1383eade4bf4986c7b11501baa800.png) be linearly independent eigenvectors of the matrix
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14041802/assets/1afe535b20d0fd1ce03b2b0886424a5ef1a29f4eea7e47c1aa818af67c98e868.png)
Given that $\lambda_1=4+5\textrm{i}$ is an eigenvalue of $A,$ find the value of ${\dfrac{a_1a_2}{b_1b_2}}.$
e-5529.worked_solution:
To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation 

$$
(A - \lambda I) \textbf{x}=\mathbf{0}.
$$

 

In our case, we have $\,\lambda_1 =4+5\textrm{i}$ and

$$
\begin{aligned}A-{\lambda }_{1}I & =[\begin{aligned}4 & 5 \\ -5 & 4\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}4+5\text{i} & 0 \\ 0 & 4+5\text{i}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-5\text{i} & 5 \\ -5 & -5\text{i}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the homogeneous system of linear equations

$$
{\begin{aligned}-5\text{i}{x}_{1}+5{x}_{2}=0 \\ -5{x}_{1}-5\text{i}{x}_{2}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since the matrix $A-(4+5\textrm{i})I$ is singular, the system above must have a non-zero solution. This means that one equation of the system is a multiple of another.

As a result, we can drop one of the rows and take one of the variables as the free variable. For example, from the first equation, we get

$$
x_2 = \textrm{i}x_1.
$$

So, the general solution is given by

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14041802/assets/af8f52f23a6fdcd1f070eff5876415cc884ffaafcbb2fe3f8737c31cc4761c86.png)

Setting $x_1=1,$ we get the eigenvector

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14041802/assets/65c073a60a27234349281e873958c2c9d54fb703331a4de23cc358a3eab1b232.png) 

Now, since $\lambda_1=4+5\textrm{i}$ is a complex eigenvalue of $A,$ the second eigenvalue of $A$ must be the complex conjugate of $\lambda_1.$ Therefore, we have 

$$
\lambda_2=\overline{\lambda_1}=4-5\textrm{i}.
$$

Moreover, the corresponding eigenvector must be the complex conjugate of $\mathbf v_1.$ Therefore, we have

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14041802/assets/ca11ae0cca8d07c026108e71b96398171597f7330cb2390d871a8071e7bba873.png)

Finally, we obtain

$$
{\dfrac{a_1a_2}{b_1b_2}} = {\dfrac{(1)(1)}{(\textrm{i})(-\textrm{i})}} = 1.
$$

EXPLANATION

The eigenvectors are non-zero vectors v such that Av=λv. So, we have

Av=[−44−84][1+i2]=[4−4i−8i]=[−4i2−4i−8i]=−4i[1+i2]=−4iv.

content.problem:
Determine if $v=[\begin{aligned}1+\text{i} \\ 2\end{aligned}]$ is an eigenvector of the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}-4 & 4 \\ -8 & 4\end{aligned}].$
If so, then what is the corresponding eigenvalue?
content.worked_solution:
The eigenvectors are non-zero vectors $v$ such that $Av=\lambda v.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Av & =[\begin{aligned}-4 & 4 \\ -8 & 4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1+\text{i} \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4-4\text{i} \\ -8\text{i}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-4{\text{i}}^{2}-4\text{i} \\ -8\text{i}\end{aligned}] \\  & =-4\text{i}[\begin{aligned}1+\text{i} \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =-4\text{i}v.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $Av=-4\text{i}v,$ we conclude that $v$ is an eigenvector of $A$ and the corresponding eigenvalue is $\lambda =-4\text{i}.$

decision.explanation: Multiplying gives Av=[4i,4-4i]^T. Since 2i[2,-2-2i]^T=[4i,4-4i]^T, Av=2iv. Therefore v is an eigenvector with eigenvalue 2i.

after.name: Question 2
after.problem: Determine whether $v=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -2-2\text{i}\end{aligned}]$ is an eigenvector of the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}-2 & -2 \\ 4 & 2\end{aligned}].$ If so, then what is the corresponding eigenvalue?
after.worked_solution:
The eigenvectors of $A$ are the non-zero vectors $v$ such that $Av=\lambda v.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Av & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & -2 \\ 4 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 \\ -2-2\text{i}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4\text{i} \\ 4-4\text{i}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4\text{i} \\ -4{\text{i}}^{2}-4\text{i}\end{aligned}] \\  & =2\text{i}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -2-2\text{i}\end{aligned}] \\  & =2\text{i}v.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $Av=2\text{i}v,$ we conclude that $v$ is an eigenvector of $A$ and the corresponding eigenvalue is $\lambda =2\text{i}.$

after.name: Question 3
after.problem:
Determine whether $v=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -2-2\text{i}\end{aligned}]$ is an eigenvector of the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}-3 & -3 \\ 6 & 3\end{aligned}].$
If so, then what is the corresponding eigenvalue?
after.worked_solution:
The eigenvectors of $A$ are the non-zero vectors $v$ such that $Av=\lambda v.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Av & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & -3 \\ 6 & 3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 \\ -2-2\text{i}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}6\text{i} \\ 6-6\text{i}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}6\text{i} \\ -6{\text{i}}^{2}-6\text{i}\end{aligned}] \\  & =3\text{i}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -2-2\text{i}\end{aligned}] \\  & =3\text{i}v.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $Av=3\text{i}v,$ we conclude that $v$ is an eigenvector of $A$ and the corresponding eigenvalue is $\lambda =3\text{i}.$

Question 3

Determine whether v=[2−2−2i] is an eigenvector of the matrix A=[−3−363]. If so, then what is the corresponding eigenvalue?

a
λ=3
b
λ=i
c
λ=3i
d
v is not an eigenvector of A
e
λ=−3i
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The eigenvectors of A are the non-zero vectors v such that Av=λv. So, we have

Av=[−3−363][2−2−2i]=[6i6−6i]=[6i−6i2−6i]=3i[2−2−2i]=3iv.

Since Av=3iv, we conclude that v is an eigenvector of A and the corresponding eigenvalue is λ=3i.

content.knowledge_point: Finding a Complex Eigenvalue of a Matrix Given a Complex Eigenvector
content.problem:
Determine whether $v=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -2-2\text{i}\end{aligned}]$ is an eigenvector of the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}-3 & -3 \\ 6 & 3\end{aligned}].$
If so, then what is the corresponding eigenvalue?
content.worked_solution:
The eigenvectors of $A$ are the non-zero vectors $v$ such that $Av=\lambda v.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Av & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & -3 \\ 6 & 3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 \\ -2-2\text{i}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}6\text{i} \\ 6-6\text{i}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}6\text{i} \\ -6{\text{i}}^{2}-6\text{i}\end{aligned}] \\  & =3\text{i}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -2-2\text{i}\end{aligned}] \\  & =3\text{i}v.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $Av=3\text{i}v,$ we conclude that $v$ is an eigenvector of $A$ and the corresponding eigenvalue is $\lambda =3\text{i}.$

$$

Since $Av=7\text{i}v,$ we conclude that $v$ is an eigenvector of $A$ and the corresponding eigenvalue is $\lambda =7\text{i}.$

after.name: Question 5
after.problem:
Determine if $v=[\begin{aligned}-\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}]$ is an eigenvector of the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}].$
If so, then what is the corresponding eigenvalue?
after.worked_solution:
The eigenvectors are non-zero vectors $v$ such that $Av=\lambda v.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Av & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1-\text{i} \\ 1+\text{i}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-{\text{i}}^{2}-\text{i} \\ 1+\text{i}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-\text{i}(\text{i}+1) \\ 1+\text{i}\end{aligned}] \\  & =(1+\text{i})[\begin{aligned}-\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =(1+\text{i})v.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $Av=(1+\text{i})v,$ we conclude that $v$ is an eigenvector of $A$ and the corresponding eigenvalue is $\lambda =1+\text{i}.$

decision.explanation: The first row of Av=λv gives a+b=√3 i a, so b=(√3 i−1)a. Here a cannot be zero, since that would also force b=0. Therefore b/a=√3 i−1.

after.name: Question 6
after.problem:
If $v=[\begin{aligned}a \\ b\end{aligned}]$ is an eigenvector of 
$A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -4 & -1\end{aligned}]$
that corresponds to the eigenvalue $\lambda =\sqrt{3}\text{i},$
then what is the value of $\frac{b}{a}?$
after.worked_solution:
To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation 

$$
(A-\lambda I)\text{x}=0.
$$

 

In our case, we have $\,\lambda =\sqrt{3}\text{i},$ and

$$
\begin{aligned}A-\lambda I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -4 & -1\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}\sqrt{3}\text{i} & 0 \\ 0 & \sqrt{3}\text{i}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1-\sqrt{3}\text{i} & 1 \\ -4 & -1-\sqrt{3}\text{i}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the homogeneous system of linear equations

$$
{\begin{aligned}(1-\sqrt{3}\text{i}){x}_{1}+{x}_{2}=0 \\ -4{x}_{1}+(-1-\sqrt{3}\text{i}){x}_{2}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since the matrix $A-\sqrt{3}\text{i}I$ is singular, the system above must have a non-zero solution. This means that one equation of the system is a multiple of another. As a result, we can drop one of the rows and take one of the variables to be the free variable. For example, from the first equation, we get

$$
{x}_{2}=-(1-\sqrt{3}\text{i}){x}_{1}
$$

Therefore, the general solution is given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ -(1-\sqrt{3}\text{i}){x}_{1}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{1}\in C.
$$

Setting ${x}_{1}=-1,$ we get the eigenvector 

$$
v=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1-\sqrt{3}\text{i}\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, $\frac{b}{a}=\frac{1-\sqrt{3}\text{i}}{-1}=\sqrt{3}\text{i}-1.$

Question 6

If v=[ab] is an eigenvector of A=[11−4−1] that corresponds to the eigenvalue λ=3i, then what is the value of ba?

a
2i−1
b
1−3i
c
2+4i
d
3i−1
e
34i−14
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation (A−λI)x=0.

In our case, we have λ=3i, and

A−λI=[11−4−1]−[3i003i]=[1−3i1−4−1−3i].

So, we have the homogeneous system of linear equations

{(1−3i)x1+x2=0−4x1+(−1−3i)x2=0.

Now, since the matrix A−3iI is singular, the system above must have a non-zero solution. This means that one equation of the system is a multiple of another. As a result, we can drop one of the rows and take one of the variables to be the free variable. For example, from the first equation, we get

x2=−(1−3i)x1

Therefore, the general solution is given by

[x1−(1−3i)x1],x1∈C.

Setting x1=−1, we get the eigenvector

v=[−11−3i].

Finally, ba=1−3i−1=3i−1.

content.knowledge_point: Finding a Complex Eigenvector of a Matrix Given a Complex Eigenvalue
content.problem:
If $v=[\begin{aligned}a \\ b\end{aligned}]$ is an eigenvector of 
$A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -4 & -1\end{aligned}]$
that corresponds to the eigenvalue $\lambda =\sqrt{3}\text{i},$
then what is the value of $\frac{b}{a}?$
content.worked_solution:
To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation 

$$
(A-\lambda I)\text{x}=0.
$$

 

In our case, we have $\,\lambda =\sqrt{3}\text{i},$ and

$$
\begin{aligned}A-\lambda I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -4 & -1\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}\sqrt{3}\text{i} & 0 \\ 0 & \sqrt{3}\text{i}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1-\sqrt{3}\text{i} & 1 \\ -4 & -1-\sqrt{3}\text{i}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the homogeneous system of linear equations

$$
{\begin{aligned}(1-\sqrt{3}\text{i}){x}_{1}+{x}_{2}=0 \\ -4{x}_{1}+(-1-\sqrt{3}\text{i}){x}_{2}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since the matrix $A-\sqrt{3}\text{i}I$ is singular, the system above must have a non-zero solution. This means that one equation of the system is a multiple of another. As a result, we can drop one of the rows and take one of the variables to be the free variable. For example, from the first equation, we get

$$
{x}_{2}=-(1-\sqrt{3}\text{i}){x}_{1}
$$

Therefore, the general solution is given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ -(1-\sqrt{3}\text{i}){x}_{1}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{1}\in C.
$$

Setting ${x}_{1}=-1,$ we get the eigenvector 

$$
v=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1-\sqrt{3}\text{i}\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, $\frac{b}{a}=\frac{1-\sqrt{3}\text{i}}{-1}=\sqrt{3}\text{i}-1.$

after.name: Question 7
after.problem:
If $v=[\begin{aligned}a \\ b\end{aligned}]$ is an eigenvector of 
$A=[\begin{aligned}3 & 5 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}]$
that corresponds to the eigenvalue $\lambda =2+3\text{i},$
then what is the value of $\frac{a}{b}?$
after.worked_solution:
To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation 

$$
(A-\lambda I)\text{x}=0.
$$

 

In our case, we have $\,\lambda =2+3\text{i},$ and

$$
\begin{aligned}A-\lambda I & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 5 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}2+3\text{i} & 0 \\ 0 & 2+3\text{i}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1-3\text{i} & 5 \\ -2 & -1-3\text{i}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the homogeneous system of linear equations

$$
{\begin{aligned}(1-3\text{i}){x}_{1}+5{x}_{2}=0 \\ -2{x}_{1}+(-1-3\text{i}){x}_{2}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since the matrix $A-(2+3\text{i})I$ is singular, the system above must have a non-zero solution. This means that one equation of the system is a multiple of another. As a result, we can drop one of the rows and take one of the variables to be the free variable. For example, from the second equation, we get

$$
{x}_{1}=-\frac{1}{2}(1+3\text{i}){x}_{2}
$$

Question 7

If v=[ab] is an eigenvector of A=[35−21] that corresponds to the eigenvalue λ=2+3i, then what is the value of ab?

a
12−32i
b
1−3i
c
−12−32i
d
−12+32i
e
12+32i
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation (A−λI)x=0.

In our case, we have λ=2+3i, and

A−λI=[35−21]−[2+3i002+3i]=[1−3i5−2−1−3i].

So, we have the homogeneous system of linear equations

{(1−3i)x1+5x2=0−2x1+(−1−3i)x2=0.

Now, since the matrix A−(2+3i)I is singular, the system above must have a non-zero solution. This means that one equation of the system is a multiple of another. As a result, we can drop one of the rows and take one of the variables to be the free variable. For example, from the second equation, we get

x1=−12(1+3i)x2

Therefore, the general solution is given by

[−12(1+3i)x2x2],x2∈C.

Setting x2=−2, we get the eigenvector

v=[1+3i−2].

Finally, ab=−1+3i2=−12−32i.

content.knowledge_point: Finding a Complex Eigenvector of a Matrix Given a Complex Eigenvalue
content.problem:
If $v=[\begin{aligned}a \\ b\end{aligned}]$ is an eigenvector of 
$A=[\begin{aligned}3 & 5 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}]$
that corresponds to the eigenvalue $\lambda =2+3\text{i},$
then what is the value of $\frac{a}{b}?$
content.worked_solution:
To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation 

$$
(A-\lambda I)\text{x}=0.
$$

 

In our case, we have $\,\lambda =2+3\text{i},$ and

$$
\begin{aligned}A-\lambda I & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 5 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}2+3\text{i} & 0 \\ 0 & 2+3\text{i}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1-3\text{i} & 5 \\ -2 & -1-3\text{i}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the homogeneous system of linear equations

$$
{\begin{aligned}(1-3\text{i}){x}_{1}+5{x}_{2}=0 \\ -2{x}_{1}+(-1-3\text{i}){x}_{2}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since the matrix $A-(2+3\text{i})I$ is singular, the system above must have a non-zero solution. This means that one equation of the system is a multiple of another. As a result, we can drop one of the rows and take one of the variables to be the free variable. For example, from the second equation, we get

$$
{x}_{1}=-\frac{1}{2}(1+3\text{i}){x}_{2}
$$

Therefore, the general solution is given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{2}(1+3\text{i}){x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in C.
$$

Setting ${x}_{2}=-2,$ we get the eigenvector 

$$
v=[\begin{aligned}1+3\text{i} \\ -2\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, $\frac{a}{b}=-\frac{1+3\text{i}}{2}=-\frac{1}{2}-\frac{3}{2}\text{i}.$

content.knowledge_point: Finding a Complex Eigenvector of a Matrix Given a Complex Eigenvalue
content.problem:
If $v=[\begin{aligned}a \\ b\end{aligned}]$ is an eigenvector of 
$A=[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ -3 & 2\end{aligned}]$
that corresponds to the eigenvalue $\lambda =2-3\text{i},$
then what is the value of $\frac{a}{b}?$
content.worked_solution:
To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation 

$$
(A-\lambda I)\text{x}=0.
$$

 

In our case, we have $\,\lambda =2-3\text{i},$ and

$$
\begin{aligned}A-\lambda I & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ -3 & 2\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}2-3\text{i} & 0 \\ 0 & 2-3\text{i}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3\text{i} & 3 \\ -3 & 3\text{i}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the homogeneous system of linear equations

$$
{\begin{aligned}3\text{i}{x}_{1}+3{x}_{2}=0 \\ -3{x}_{1}+3\text{i}{x}_{2}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since the matrix $A-(2-3\text{i})I$ is singular, the system above must have a non-zero solution. This means that one equation of the system is a multiple of another. As a result, we can drop one of the rows and take one of the variables to be the free variable. For example, from the second equation, we get

$$
{x}_{1}=\text{i}{x}_{2}
$$

Therefore, the general solution is given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}\text{i}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in C.
$$

Setting ${x}_{2}=1,$ we get the eigenvector 

$$
v=[\begin{aligned}\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, $\frac{a}{b}=\frac{\text{i}}{1}=\text{i}.$

after.name: Question 9
after.problem:
If $v=[\begin{aligned}a \\ b\end{aligned}]$ is an eigenvector of 
$A=[\begin{aligned}-5 & -2 \\ 5 & 1\end{aligned}]$
that corresponds to the eigenvalue $\lambda =-2+\text{i},$
then what is the value of $\frac{b}{a}?$
after.worked_solution:
To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation 

$$
(A-\lambda I)\text{x}=0.
$$

 

In our case, we have $\,\lambda =-2+\text{i},$ and

$$
\begin{aligned}A-\lambda I & =[\begin{aligned}-5 & -2 \\ 5 & 1\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}-2+\text{i} & 0 \\ 0 & -2+\text{i}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-3-\text{i} & -2 \\ 5 & 3-\text{i}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the homogeneous system of linear equations

$$
{\begin{aligned}(-3-\text{i}){x}_{1}-2{x}_{2}=0 \\ 5{x}_{1}+(3-\text{i}){x}_{2}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since the matrix $A-(-2+\text{i})I$ is singular, the system above must have a non-zero solution. This means that one equation of the system is a multiple of another. As a result, we can drop one of the rows and take one of the variables to be the free variable. For example, from the second equation, we get

$$
{x}_{1}=-\frac{1}{5}(3-\text{i}){x}_{2}
$$

Therefore, the general solution is given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{5}(3-\text{i}){x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in C.
$$

Setting ${x}_{2}=-5,$ we get the eigenvector 

$$
v=[\begin{aligned}3-\text{i} \\ -5\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, $\frac{b}{a}=\frac{-5}{3-\text{i}}=\frac{-5(3+\text{i})}{10}=-\frac{3}{2}-\frac{1}{2}\text{i}.$

Question 9
?

If v=[ab] is an eigenvector of A=[−5−251] that corresponds to the eigenvalue λ=−2+i, then what is the value of ba?

a
−32−12i
b
12−12i
c
32+i
d
−32−32i
e
−35+15i
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation (A−λI)x=0.

In our case, we have λ=−2+i, and

A−λI=[−5−251]−[−2+i00−2+i]=[−3−i−253−i].

So, we have the homogeneous system of linear equations

{(−3−i)x1−2x2=05x1+(3−i)x2=0.

Now, since the matrix A−(−2+i)I is singular, the system above must have a non-zero solution. This means that one equation of the system is a multiple of another. As a result, we can drop one of the rows and take one of the variables to be the free variable. For example, from the second equation, we get

x1=−15(3−i)x2

Therefore, the general solution is given by

[−15(3−i)x2x2],x2∈C.

Setting x2=−5, we get the eigenvector

v=[3−i−5].

Finally, ba=−53−i=−5(3+i)10=−32−12i.

content.knowledge_point: Finding a Complex Eigenvector of a Matrix Given a Complex Eigenvalue
content.problem:
If $v=[\begin{aligned}a \\ b\end{aligned}]$ is an eigenvector of 
$A=[\begin{aligned}-5 & -2 \\ 5 & 1\end{aligned}]$
that corresponds to the eigenvalue $\lambda =-2+\text{i},$
then what is the value of $\frac{b}{a}?$
content.worked_solution:
To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation 

$$
(A-\lambda I)\text{x}=0.
$$

 

In our case, we have $\,\lambda =-2+\text{i},$ and

$$
\begin{aligned}A-\lambda I & =[\begin{aligned}-5 & -2 \\ 5 & 1\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}-2+\text{i} & 0 \\ 0 & -2+\text{i}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-3-\text{i} & -2 \\ 5 & 3-\text{i}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the homogeneous system of linear equations

$$
{\begin{aligned}(-3-\text{i}){x}_{1}-2{x}_{2}=0 \\ 5{x}_{1}+(3-\text{i}){x}_{2}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since the matrix $A-(-2+\text{i})I$ is singular, the system above must have a non-zero solution. This means that one equation of the system is a multiple of another. As a result, we can drop one of the rows and take one of the variables to be the free variable. For example, from the second equation, we get

$$
{x}_{1}=-\frac{1}{5}(3-\text{i}){x}_{2}
$$

Therefore, the general solution is given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{5}(3-\text{i}){x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in C.
$$

Setting ${x}_{2}=-5,$ we get the eigenvector 

$$
v=[\begin{aligned}3-\text{i} \\ -5\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, $\frac{b}{a}=\frac{-5}{3-\text{i}}=\frac{-5(3+\text{i})}{10}=-\frac{3}{2}-\frac{1}{2}\text{i}.$

after.problem:
If $v=[\begin{aligned}a \\ b\end{aligned}]$ is an eigenvector of 
$A=[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 \\ -3 & -2\end{aligned}]$
that corresponds to the eigenvalue $\lambda =-\sqrt{2}\text{i},$
then what is the value of $\frac{a}{b}?$
after.worked_solution:
To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation 

$$
(A-\lambda I)\text{x}=0.
$$

 

In our case, we have $\,\lambda =-\sqrt{2}\text{i},$ and

$$
\begin{aligned}A-\lambda I & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 \\ -3 & -2\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}-\sqrt{2}\text{i} & 0 \\ 0 & -\sqrt{2}\text{i}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2+\sqrt{2}\text{i} & 2 \\ -3 & -2+\sqrt{2}\text{i}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the homogeneous system of linear equations

$$
{\begin{aligned}(2+\sqrt{2}\text{i}){x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}=0 \\ -3{x}_{1}+(-2+\sqrt{2}\text{i}){x}_{2}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since the matrix $A-(-\sqrt{2}\text{i})I$ is singular, the system above must have a non-zero solution. This means that one equation of the system is a multiple of another. As a result, we can drop one of the rows and take one of the variables to be the free variable. For example, from the first equation, we get

$$
{x}_{2}=-\frac{1}{2}(2+\sqrt{2}\text{i}){x}_{1}
$$

Therefore, the general solution is given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ -\frac{1}{2}(2+\sqrt{2}\text{i}){x}_{1}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{1}\in C.
$$

Setting ${x}_{1}=-2,$ we get the eigenvector 

$$
v=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 2+\sqrt{2}\text{i}\end{aligned}].
$$

To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation (A−λI)x=0.

In our case, we have λ=−2i, and

A−λI=[22−3−2]−[−2i00−2i]=[2+2i2−3−2+2i].

So, we have the homogeneous system of linear equations

{(2+2i)x1+2x2=0−3x1+(−2+2i)x2=0.

Now, since the matrix A−(−2i)I is singular, the system above must have a non-zero solution. This means that one equation of the system is a multiple of another. As a result, we can drop one of the rows and take one of the variables to be the free variable. For example, from the first equation, we get

x2=−12(2+2i)x1

Therefore, the general solution is given by

[x1−12(2+2i)x1],x1∈C.

Setting x1=−2, we get the eigenvector

v=[−22+2i].

Finally, ab=−22+2i=−2(2−2i)6=−23+23i.

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A-\lambda I) & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}7-\lambda  & 5 \\ -4 & 3-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (7-\lambda )(3-\lambda )-(-4)(5) & =0 \\ 21-7\lambda -3\lambda +{\lambda }^{2}+20 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-10\lambda +41 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Using the quadratic formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\lambda  & =\frac{-b\pm \sqrt{{b}^{2}-4ac}}{2a} \\  & =\frac{10\pm \sqrt{(-10)^{2}-4(1)(41)}}{2(1)} \\  & =\frac{10\pm \sqrt{-64}}{2} \\  & =\frac{10\pm 8\text{i}}{2} \\  & =5\pm 4\text{i}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the eigenvalues are $\lambda =5\pm 4\text{i}.$

Now, let's consider the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=5+4\text{i}.$ We have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-{\lambda }_{1}I & =[\begin{aligned}7 & 5 \\ -4 & 3\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}5+4\text{i} & 0 \\ 0 & 5+4\text{i}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2-4\text{i} & 5 \\ -4 & -2-4\text{i}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}

$$

$$
{x}_{2}=(-\frac{2}{5}+\frac{4}{5}\text{i}){x}_{1}
$$

$$

$$

$$

content.problem:
Given that ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}{a}_{1} \\ {b}_{1}\end{aligned}]$ and ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}{a}_{2} \\ {b}_{2}\end{aligned}]$ are linearly independent eigenvectors of the matrix
$A=[\begin{aligned}7 & 5 \\ -4 & 3\end{aligned}],$
what is the value of $\frac{{a}_{1}{a}_{2}}{{b}_{1}{b}_{2}}?$
content.worked_solution:
First, we need to find the eigenvalues of $A.$ To do that, we must solve the characteristic equation $det(A-\lambda I)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A-\lambda I) & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}7-\lambda  & 5 \\ -4 & 3-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (7-\lambda )(3-\lambda )-(-4)(5) & =0 \\ 21-7\lambda -3\lambda +{\lambda }^{2}+20 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-10\lambda +41 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Using the quadratic formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\lambda  & =\frac{-b\pm \sqrt{{b}^{2}-4ac}}{2a} \\  & =\frac{10\pm \sqrt{(-10)^{2}-4(1)(41)}}{2(1)} \\  & =\frac{10\pm \sqrt{-64}}{2} \\  & =\frac{10\pm 8\text{i}}{2} \\  & =5\pm 4\text{i}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the eigenvalues are $\lambda =5\pm 4\text{i}.$

Now, let's consider the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=5+4\text{i}.$ We have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-{\lambda }_{1}I & =[\begin{aligned}7 & 5 \\ -4 & 3\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}5+4\text{i} & 0 \\ 0 & 5+4\text{i}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2-4\text{i} & 5 \\ -4 & -2-4\text{i}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, we get the system of linear equations

$$
{\begin{aligned}(2-4\text{i}){x}_{1}+5{x}_{2}=0 \\ -4{x}_{1}+(-2-4\text{i}){x}_{2}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since the matrix $A-(5+4\text{i})I$ is singular, the system above must have a non-zero solution. This means that one equation of the system is a multiple of another. As a result, we can drop one of the rows and take one of the variables as the free variable. For example, from the first equation, we get

$$
{x}_{2}=(-\frac{2}{5}+\frac{4}{5}\text{i}){x}_{1}
$$

Hence, the general solution is given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ (-\frac{2}{5}+\frac{4}{5}\text{i}){x}_{1}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{1}\in C.
$$

Setting ${x}_{1}=5,$ we get the eigenvector

$$
{v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}5 \\ -2+4\text{i}\end{aligned}].
$$

 

Then, to compute the second eigenvector corresponding to ${\lambda }_{2}=5-4\text{i}$, we simply compute the complex conjugate of ${\overset{―}{v}}_{1},$ and get

$$
{v}_{2}={\overset{―}{v}}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}5 \\ -2-4\text{i}\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{a}_{1}{a}_{2}}{{b}_{1}{b}_{2}} & =\frac{(5)(5)}{(-2+4\text{i})(-2-4\text{i})}=\frac{5}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

$$

$$

$$
{\begin{aligned}(-5-5\text{i}){x}_{1}-5{x}_{2}=0 \\ 10{x}_{1}+(5-5\text{i}){x}_{2}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since the matrix $A-(1+5\text{i})I$ is singular, the system above must have a non-zero solution. This means that one equation of the system is a multiple of another. As a result, we can drop one of the rows and take one of the variables as the free variable. For example, from the second equation, we get

$$
{x}_{1}=-\frac{1}{2}(1-\text{i}){x}_{2}
$$

Hence, the general solution is given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{2}(1-\text{i}){x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in C.
$$

Setting ${x}_{2}=-2,$ we get the eigenvector

$$
{v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1-\text{i} \\ -2\end{aligned}].
$$

On the other hand, since ${\lambda }_{1}=1+5\text{i}$ is a complex eigenvalue of $A,$ the second eigenvalue of $A$ must be the complex conjugate of ${\lambda }_{1}.$ Therefore, 

$$
{\lambda }_{2}=\overset{―}{{\lambda }_{1}}=1-5\text{i}.
$$

Moreover, the corresponding eigenvector to ${\lambda }_{2}$ is

$$
{v}_{2}={\overset{―}{v}}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1+\text{i} \\ -2\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we obtain

$$
\frac{{a}_{1}{a}_{2}}{{b}_{1}{b}_{2}}=\frac{(1-\text{i})(1+\text{i})}{(-2)(-2)}=\frac{1}{2}.
$$

To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation (A−λI)x=0.

Now, since the matrix A−(1+5i)I is singular, the system above must have a non-zero solution. This means that one equation of the system is a multiple of another. As a result, we can drop one of the rows and take one of the variables as the free variable. For example, from the second equation, we get

content.knowledge_point: Finding Two Linearly Independent Complex Eigenvectors of a 2x2 Matrix
content.problem:
Let ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}{a}_{1} \\ {b}_{1}\end{aligned}]$ and ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}{a}_{2} \\ {b}_{2}\end{aligned}]$ be linearly independent eigenvectors of the matrix
$A=[\begin{aligned}-4 & -5 \\ 10 & 6\end{aligned}].$
Given that ${\lambda }_{1}=1+5\text{i}$ is an eigenvalue of $A,$ find the value of $\frac{{a}_{1}{a}_{2}}{{b}_{1}{b}_{2}}.$
content.worked_solution:
To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation 

$$
(A-\lambda I)\text{x}=0.
$$

 

In our case, we have $\,{\lambda }_{1}=1+5\text{i}$ and

$$
\begin{aligned}A-{\lambda }_{1}I & =[\begin{aligned}-4 & -5 \\ 10 & 6\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1+5\text{i} & 0 \\ 0 & 1+5\text{i}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-5-5\text{i} & -5 \\ 10 & 5-5\text{i}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the homogeneous system of linear equations

$$
{\begin{aligned}(-5-5\text{i}){x}_{1}-5{x}_{2}=0 \\ 10{x}_{1}+(5-5\text{i}){x}_{2}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since the matrix $A-(1+5\text{i})I$ is singular, the system above must have a non-zero solution. This means that one equation of the system is a multiple of another. As a result, we can drop one of the rows and take one of the variables as the free variable. For example, from the second equation, we get

$$
{x}_{1}=-\frac{1}{2}(1-\text{i}){x}_{2}
$$

Hence, the general solution is given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{2}(1-\text{i}){x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in C.
$$

Setting ${x}_{2}=-2,$ we get the eigenvector

$$
{v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1-\text{i} \\ -2\end{aligned}].
$$

On the other hand, since ${\lambda }_{1}=1+5\text{i}$ is a complex eigenvalue of $A,$ the second eigenvalue of $A$ must be the complex conjugate of ${\lambda }_{1}.$ Therefore, 

$$
{\lambda }_{2}=\overset{―}{{\lambda }_{1}}=1-5\text{i}.
$$

Moreover, the corresponding eigenvector to ${\lambda }_{2}$ is

$$
{v}_{2}={\overset{―}{v}}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1+\text{i} \\ -2\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we obtain

$$
\frac{{a}_{1}{a}_{2}}{{b}_{1}{b}_{2}}=\frac{(1-\text{i})(1+\text{i})}{(-2)(-2)}=\frac{1}{2}.
$$

$$

$$
{x}_{1}=\frac{1}{5}(1-3\text{i}){x}_{2}

[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{5}(1-3\text{i}){x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in C.

$$

Let v1=[a1b1] and v2=[a2b2] be linearly independent eigenvectors of the matrix A=[−32−5−1]. Given that λ1=−2+3i is an eigenvalue of A, find the value of a1a2b1b2.

a
25
b
15
c

109
e

Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation (A−λI)x=0.

In our case, we have λ1=−2+3i and

A−λ1I=[−32−5−1]−[−2+3i00−2+3i]=[−1−3i2−51−3i].

So, we have the homogeneous system of linear equations

{(−1−3i)x1+2x2=0−5x1+(1−3i)x2=0.

Now, since the matrix A−(−2+3i)I is singular, the system above must have a non-zero solution. This means that one equation of the system is a multiple of another. As a result, we can drop one of the rows and take one of the variables as the free variable. For example, from the second equation, we get

x1=15(1−3i)x2

Hence, the general solution is given by

[15(1−3i)x2x2],x2∈C.

Setting x2=5, we get the eigenvector

v1=[1−3i5].

On the other hand, since λ1=−2+3i is a complex eigenvalue of A, the second eigenvalue of A must be the complex conjugate of λ1. Therefore,

λ2=λ1―=−2−3i.

Moreover, the corresponding eigenvector to λ2 is

v2=v―1=[1+3i5].

Therefore, we obtain

a1a2b1b2=(1−3i)(1+3i)(5)(5)=25.

content.knowledge_point: Finding Two Linearly Independent Complex Eigenvectors of a 2x2 Matrix
content.problem:
Let ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}{a}_{1} \\ {b}_{1}\end{aligned}]$ and ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}{a}_{2} \\ {b}_{2}\end{aligned}]$ be linearly independent eigenvectors of the matrix
$A=[\begin{aligned}-3 & 2 \\ -5 & -1\end{aligned}].$
Given that ${\lambda }_{1}=-2+3\text{i}$ is an eigenvalue of $A,$ find the value of $\frac{{a}_{1}{a}_{2}}{{b}_{1}{b}_{2}}.$
content.worked_solution:
To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation 

$$
(A-\lambda I)\text{x}=0.
$$

 

In our case, we have $\,{\lambda }_{1}=-2+3\text{i}$ and

$$
\begin{aligned}A-{\lambda }_{1}I & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & 2 \\ -5 & -1\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}-2+3\text{i} & 0 \\ 0 & -2+3\text{i}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1-3\text{i} & 2 \\ -5 & 1-3\text{i}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the homogeneous system of linear equations

$$
{\begin{aligned}(-1-3\text{i}){x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}=0 \\ -5{x}_{1}+(1-3\text{i}){x}_{2}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since the matrix $A-(-2+3\text{i})I$ is singular, the system above must have a non-zero solution. This means that one equation of the system is a multiple of another. As a result, we can drop one of the rows and take one of the variables as the free variable. For example, from the second equation, we get

$$
{x}_{1}=\frac{1}{5}(1-3\text{i}){x}_{2}
$$

Hence, the general solution is given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{5}(1-3\text{i}){x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in C.
$$

Setting ${x}_{2}=5,$ we get the eigenvector

$$
{v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1-3\text{i} \\ 5\end{aligned}].
$$

On the other hand, since ${\lambda }_{1}=-2+3\text{i}$ is a complex eigenvalue of $A,$ the second eigenvalue of $A$ must be the  complex conjugate of ${\lambda }_{1}.$ Therefore, 

$$
{\lambda }_{2}=\overset{―}{{\lambda }_{1}}=-2-3\text{i}.
$$

Moreover, the corresponding eigenvector to ${\lambda }_{2}$ is

$$
{v}_{2}={\overset{―}{v}}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1+3\text{i} \\ 5\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we obtain

$$
\frac{{a}_{1}{a}_{2}}{{b}_{1}{b}_{2}}=\frac{(1-3\text{i})(1+3\text{i})}{(5)(5)}=\frac{2}{5}.
$$

decision.explanation: The characteristic polynomial is λ²−2λ+10, so the eigenvalues are 1±3i. From 5a+5b=λa, b/a=(λ−5)/5. Thus the requested product is ((−4+3i)/5)((−4−3i)/5)=(16+9)/25=1.

after.name: Question 14
after.problem:
Given that ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}{a}_{1} \\ {b}_{1}\end{aligned}]$ and ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}{a}_{2} \\ {b}_{2}\end{aligned}]$ are linearly independent eigenvectors of the matrix
$A=[\begin{aligned}5 & 5 \\ -5 & -3\end{aligned}],$
what is the value of $\frac{{b}_{1}{b}_{2}}{{a}_{1}{a}_{2}}?$
after.worked_solution:
First, we need to find the eigenvalues of $A.$ To do that, we must solve the characteristic equation $det(A-\lambda I)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A-\lambda I) & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}5-\lambda  & 5 \\ -5 & -3-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (5-\lambda )(-3-\lambda )-(-5)(5) & =0 \\ -15-5\lambda +3\lambda +{\lambda }^{2}+25 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-2\lambda +10 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Using the quadratic formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\lambda  & =\frac{-b\pm \sqrt{{b}^{2}-4ac}}{2a} \\  & =\frac{-(-2)\pm \sqrt{(-2)^{2}-4(1)(10)}}{2(1)} \\  & =\frac{-(-2)\pm \sqrt{-36}}{2} \\  & =\frac{2\pm 6\text{i}}{2} \\  & =1\pm 3\text{i}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the eigenvalues are $\lambda =1\pm 3\text{i}.$

Now, let's consider the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=1+3\text{i}.$ We have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-{\lambda }_{1}I & =[\begin{aligned}5 & 5 \\ -5 & -3\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1+3\text{i} & 0 \\ 0 & 1+3\text{i}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4-3\text{i} & 5 \\ -5 & -4-3\text{i}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, we get the system of linear equations

$$
{\begin{aligned}(4-3\text{i}){x}_{1}+5{x}_{2}=0 \\ -5{x}_{1}+(-4-3\text{i}){x}_{2}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since the matrix $A-(1+3\text{i})I$ is singular, the system above must have a non-zero solution. This means that one equation of the system is a multiple of another. As a result, we can drop one of the rows and take one of the variables as the free variable. For example, from the second equation, we get

$$
{x}_{1}=\frac{1}{5}(-4-3\text{i}){x}_{2}
$$

Hence, the general solution is given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{5}(-4-3\text{i}){x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in C.
$$

Setting ${x}_{2}=-5,$ we get the eigenvector

$$
{v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}4+3\text{i} \\ -5\end{aligned}].
$$

 

Then, to compute the second eigenvector corresponding to ${\lambda }_{2}=1-3\text{i}$, we simply compute the complex conjugate of ${\overset{―}{v}}_{1},$ and get

$$
{v}_{2}={\overset{―}{v}}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}4-3\text{i} \\ -5\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{b}_{1}{b}_{2}}{{a}_{1}{a}_{2}} & =\frac{(-5)(-5)}{(4+3\text{i})(4-3\text{i})}=1.\end{aligned}
$$

Given that v1=[a1b1] and v2=[a2b2] are linearly independent eigenvectors of the matrix A=[55−5−3], what is the value of b1b2a1a2?

EXPLANATION

First, we need to find the eigenvalues of A. To do that, we must solve the characteristic equation det(A−λI)=0: det(A−λI)=0|5−λ5−5−3−λ|=0(5−λ)(−3−λ)−(−5)(5)=0−15−5λ+3λ+λ2+25=0λ2−2λ+10=0

Using the quadratic formula, we get

λ=−b±b2−4ac2a=−(−2)±(−2)2−4(1)(10)2(1)=−(−2)±−362=2±6i2=1±3i.

Therefore, the eigenvalues are λ=1±3i.

Now, let's consider the eigenvalue λ1=1+3i. We have

A−λ1I=[55−5−3]−[1+3i001+3i]=[4−3i5−5−4−3i].

Hence, we get the system of linear equations {(4−3i)x1+5x2=0−5x1+(−4−3i)x2=0.

Now, since the matrix A−(1+3i)I is singular, the system above must have a non-zero solution. This means that one equation of the system is a multiple of another. As a result, we can drop one of the rows and take one of the variables as the free variable. For example, from the second equation, we get

x1=15(−4−3i)x2

Hence, the general solution is given by

[15(−4−3i)x2x2],x2∈C.

Setting x2=−5, we get the eigenvector

v1=[4+3i−5].

Then, to compute the second eigenvector corresponding to λ2=1−3i, we simply compute the complex conjugate of v―1, and get

v2=v―1=[4−3i−5].

Finally, b1b2a1a2=(−5)(−5)(4+3i)(4−3i)=1.

content.knowledge_point: Finding Two Linearly Independent Complex Eigenvectors of a 2x2 Matrix
content.problem:
Given that ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}{a}_{1} \\ {b}_{1}\end{aligned}]$ and ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}{a}_{2} \\ {b}_{2}\end{aligned}]$ are linearly independent eigenvectors of the matrix
$A=[\begin{aligned}5 & 5 \\ -5 & -3\end{aligned}],$
what is the value of $\frac{{b}_{1}{b}_{2}}{{a}_{1}{a}_{2}}?$
content.worked_solution:
First, we need to find the eigenvalues of $A.$ To do that, we must solve the characteristic equation $det(A-\lambda I)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A-\lambda I) & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}5-\lambda  & 5 \\ -5 & -3-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (5-\lambda )(-3-\lambda )-(-5)(5) & =0 \\ -15-5\lambda +3\lambda +{\lambda }^{2}+25 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-2\lambda +10 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Using the quadratic formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\lambda  & =\frac{-b\pm \sqrt{{b}^{2}-4ac}}{2a} \\  & =\frac{-(-2)\pm \sqrt{(-2)^{2}-4(1)(10)}}{2(1)} \\  & =\frac{-(-2)\pm \sqrt{-36}}{2} \\  & =\frac{2\pm 6\text{i}}{2} \\  & =1\pm 3\text{i}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the eigenvalues are $\lambda =1\pm 3\text{i}.$

Now, let's consider the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=1+3\text{i}.$ We have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-{\lambda }_{1}I & =[\begin{aligned}5 & 5 \\ -5 & -3\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1+3\text{i} & 0 \\ 0 & 1+3\text{i}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4-3\text{i} & 5 \\ -5 & -4-3\text{i}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, we get the system of linear equations

$$
{\begin{aligned}(4-3\text{i}){x}_{1}+5{x}_{2}=0 \\ -5{x}_{1}+(-4-3\text{i}){x}_{2}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since the matrix $A-(1+3\text{i})I$ is singular, the system above must have a non-zero solution. This means that one equation of the system is a multiple of another. As a result, we can drop one of the rows and take one of the variables as the free variable. For example, from the second equation, we get

$$
{x}_{1}=\frac{1}{5}(-4-3\text{i}){x}_{2}
$$

Hence, the general solution is given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{5}(-4-3\text{i}){x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in C.
$$

Setting ${x}_{2}=-5,$ we get the eigenvector

$$
{v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}4+3\text{i} \\ -5\end{aligned}].
$$

 

Then, to compute the second eigenvector corresponding to ${\lambda }_{2}=1-3\text{i}$, we simply compute the complex conjugate of ${\overset{―}{v}}_{1},$ and get

$$
{v}_{2}={\overset{―}{v}}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}4-3\text{i} \\ -5\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{b}_{1}{b}_{2}}{{a}_{1}{a}_{2}} & =\frac{(-5)(-5)}{(4+3\text{i})(4-3\text{i})}=1.\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 15
after.problem:
Given that ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}{a}_{1} \\ {b}_{1}\end{aligned}]$ and ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}{a}_{2} \\ {b}_{2}\end{aligned}]$ are linearly independent eigenvectors of the matrix
$A=[\begin{aligned}-6 & -4 \\ 5 & 2\end{aligned}],$
what is the value of $\frac{{a}_{1}{a}_{2}}{{b}_{1}{b}_{2}}?$
after.worked_solution:
First, we need to find the eigenvalues of $A.$ To do that, we must solve the characteristic equation $det(A-\lambda I)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A-\lambda I) & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}-6-\lambda  & -4 \\ 5 & 2-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (-6-\lambda )(2-\lambda )-(-4)(5) & =0 \\ -12+6\lambda -2\lambda +{\lambda }^{2}+20 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+4\lambda +8 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Using the quadratic formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\lambda  & =\frac{-b\pm \sqrt{{b}^{2}-4ac}}{2a} \\  & =\frac{-4\pm \sqrt{{4}^{2}-4(1)(8)}}{2(1)} \\  & =\frac{-4\pm 4\text{i}}{2} \\  & =-2\pm 2\text{i}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the eigenvalues are $\lambda =-2\pm 2\text{i}.$

Now, let's consider the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=-2+2\text{i}.$ We have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-{\lambda }_{1}I & =[\begin{aligned}-6 & -4 \\ 5 & 2\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}-2+2\text{i} & 0 \\ 0 & -2+2\text{i}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-4-2\text{i} & -4 \\ 5 & 4-2\text{i}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, we get the system of linear equations

$$
{\begin{aligned}(-4-2\text{i}){x}_{1}-4{x}_{2}=0 \\ 5{x}_{1}+(4-2\text{i}){x}_{2}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since the matrix $A-(-2+2\text{i})I$ is singular, the system above must have a non-zero solution. This means that one equation of the system is a multiple of another. As a result, we can drop one of the rows and take one of the variables as the free variable. For example, from the first equation, we get

$$
{x}_{2}=(-1-\frac{1}{2}\text{i}){x}_{1}
$$

Hence, the general solution is given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ (-1-\frac{1}{2}\text{i}){x}_{1}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{1}\in C.
$$

Setting ${x}_{1}=2,$ we get the eigenvector

$$
{v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -2-\text{i}\end{aligned}].
$$

 

Then, to compute the second eigenvector corresponding to ${\lambda }_{2}=-2-2\text{i}$, we simply compute the complex conjugate of ${\overset{―}{v}}_{1},$ and get

$$
{v}_{2}={\overset{―}{v}}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -2+\text{i}\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{a}_{1}{a}_{2}}{{b}_{1}{b}_{2}} & =\frac{(2)(2)}{(-2-\text{i})(-2+\text{i})}=\frac{4}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Given that v1=[a1b1] and v2=[a2b2] are linearly independent eigenvectors of the matrix A=[−6−452], what is the value of a1a2b1b2?

a
45
b

Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we need to find the eigenvalues of A. To do that, we must solve the characteristic equation det(A−λI)=0: det(A−λI)=0|−6−λ−452−λ|=0(−6−λ)(2−λ)−(−4)(5)=0−12+6λ−2λ+λ2+20=0λ2+4λ+8=0

Using the quadratic formula, we get

λ=−b±b2−4ac2a=−4±42−4(1)(8)2(1)=−4±4i2=−2±2i.

Therefore, the eigenvalues are λ=−2±2i.

Now, let's consider the eigenvalue λ1=−2+2i. We have

A−λ1I=[−6−452]−[−2+2i00−2+2i]=[−4−2i−454−2i].

Hence, we get the system of linear equations {(−4−2i)x1−4x2=05x1+(4−2i)x2=0.

Now, since the matrix A−(−2+2i)I is singular, the system above must have a non-zero solution. This means that one equation of the system is a multiple of another. As a result, we can drop one of the rows and take one of the variables as the free variable. For example, from the first equation, we get

x2=(−1−12i)x1

Hence, the general solution is given by

[x1(−1−12i)x1],x1∈C.

Setting x1=2, we get the eigenvector

v1=[2−2−i].

Then, to compute the second eigenvector corresponding to λ2=−2−2i, we simply compute the complex conjugate of v―1, and get

v2=v―1=[2−2+i].

Finally, a1a2b1b2=(2)(2)(−2−i)(−2+i)=45.

content.knowledge_point: Finding Two Linearly Independent Complex Eigenvectors of a 2x2 Matrix
content.problem:
Given that ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}{a}_{1} \\ {b}_{1}\end{aligned}]$ and ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}{a}_{2} \\ {b}_{2}\end{aligned}]$ are linearly independent eigenvectors of the matrix
$A=[\begin{aligned}-6 & -4 \\ 5 & 2\end{aligned}],$
what is the value of $\frac{{a}_{1}{a}_{2}}{{b}_{1}{b}_{2}}?$
content.worked_solution:
First, we need to find the eigenvalues of $A.$ To do that, we must solve the characteristic equation $det(A-\lambda I)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A-\lambda I) & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}-6-\lambda  & -4 \\ 5 & 2-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (-6-\lambda )(2-\lambda )-(-4)(5) & =0 \\ -12+6\lambda -2\lambda +{\lambda }^{2}+20 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+4\lambda +8 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Using the quadratic formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\lambda  & =\frac{-b\pm \sqrt{{b}^{2}-4ac}}{2a} \\  & =\frac{-4\pm \sqrt{{4}^{2}-4(1)(8)}}{2(1)} \\  & =\frac{-4\pm 4\text{i}}{2} \\  & =-2\pm 2\text{i}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the eigenvalues are $\lambda =-2\pm 2\text{i}.$

Now, let's consider the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=-2+2\text{i}.$ We have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-{\lambda }_{1}I & =[\begin{aligned}-6 & -4 \\ 5 & 2\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}-2+2\text{i} & 0 \\ 0 & -2+2\text{i}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-4-2\text{i} & -4 \\ 5 & 4-2\text{i}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, we get the system of linear equations

$$
{\begin{aligned}(-4-2\text{i}){x}_{1}-4{x}_{2}=0 \\ 5{x}_{1}+(4-2\text{i}){x}_{2}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since the matrix $A-(-2+2\text{i})I$ is singular, the system above must have a non-zero solution. This means that one equation of the system is a multiple of another. As a result, we can drop one of the rows and take one of the variables as the free variable. For example, from the first equation, we get

$$
{x}_{2}=(-1-\frac{1}{2}\text{i}){x}_{1}
$$

Hence, the general solution is given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ (-1-\frac{1}{2}\text{i}){x}_{1}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{1}\in C.
$$

Setting ${x}_{1}=2,$ we get the eigenvector

$$
{v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -2-\text{i}\end{aligned}].
$$

 

Then, to compute the second eigenvector corresponding to ${\lambda }_{2}=-2-2\text{i}$, we simply compute the complex conjugate of ${\overset{―}{v}}_{1},$ and get

$$
{v}_{2}={\overset{―}{v}}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -2+\text{i}\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{a}_{1}{a}_{2}}{{b}_{1}{b}_{2}} & =\frac{(2)(2)}{(-2-\text{i})(-2+\text{i})}=\frac{4}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$
